title: An algebraic-integer congruence forces a root of unity to be one
statement: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero and let $\zeta,\alpha\in K$. Assume $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer [def-weil-algebraic-integer], meaning that it satisfies a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. Let $n\geq3$ and $r\geq1$ be integers. If $\zeta^r=1$ and $\zeta=1+n\alpha$, then $\zeta=1$.

source.place: Chapter I, Lemma 14.5, printed p.63 (PDF p.69); the root-of-unity statement over a characteristic-zero field.

proof.text: If $\zeta\ne1$, choose the least positive $m$ with $\zeta^m=1$; it exists since $r\geq1$. Then $m>1$. Choose a prime divisor $p$ of $m$, put $s=m/p$ and $\eta=\zeta^s$. We have $\eta^p=1$. For $1\leq j<p$, the equality $\eta^j=1$ would give $0<sj<m$ and $\zeta^{sj}=1$, contradicting minimality. Thus $\eta$ has order exactly $p$.

source.place: Milne, Chapter I, Lemma 14.5, printed p.63 (PDF p.69), proof: prime-order reduction and the norm equation.

proof.text: Expand $(1+n\alpha)^s$ and set $\beta=\sum_{j=1}^{s}\binom{s}{j}n^{j-1}\alpha^j$. Then $\eta=1+n\beta$. By [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure], integral elements form a subring containing the integers; hence each summand and their finite sum $\beta$ are algebraic integers. Since $n\ne0$, we also have $\beta=(\eta-1)/n\in E:=\mathbf Q(\eta)$. The same monic integer polynomial annihilates $\beta$ in $E$, because the inclusion $E\hookrightarrow K$ is injective.

source.place: Milne, Chapter I, Lemma 14.5, printed p.63 (PDF p.69), proof: prime-order reduction and the norm equation.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-prime-cyclotomic-degree-norm] to $\eta$: the field $E$ is finite over $\mathbf Q$, has degree $p-1$, and $N_{E/\mathbf Q}(\eta-1)=(-1)^{p-1}p$. Its hypotheses hold by step 1 and characteristic zero of $K$.

source.place: Milne, Chapter I, Lemma 14.5, printed p.63 (PDF p.69), proof: prime-order reduction and the norm equation.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-field-norm-preserves-integrality], $N_{E/\mathbf Q}(\beta)$ is an algebraic integer in $\mathbf Q$. Apply [lem-weil-rational-algebraic-integer] with $\Omega=\mathbf Q$ and the rational number itself as witness. Obtain $b\in\mathbf Z$ with $N_{E/\mathbf Q}(\beta)=b$.

source.place: Milne, Chapter I, Lemma 14.5, printed p.63 (PDF p.69), proof: prime-order reduction and the norm equation.

proof.text: Use multiplicativity and the scalar formula of [lem-sfb-finite-field-norm-minpoly] on $\eta-1=n\beta$: $$(-1)^{p-1}p=n^{p-1}b.$$ This is an equality of integers by injectivity of $\mathbf Z\hookrightarrow\mathbf Q$. Thus $n^{p-1}$ divides $p$. Since $p\geq2$, also $n\mid p$. Primality of $p$ and $n\geq3$ force $n=p$, hence $p\geq3$. Now $p-1\geq2$, so $p^2\mid p$, impossible for $p>1$. This contradicts $\zeta\ne1$ and proves $\zeta=1$.

source.place: Milne, Chapter I, Lemma 14.5, printed p.63 (PDF p.69), proof: prime-order reduction and the norm equation.

proof_origin.place: Milne, Chapter I, Lemma 14.5, printed p.63 (PDF p.69), proof: prime-order reduction and the norm equation.

Step 2: β=Σ_{j=1}^s C(s,j)n^{j-1}α^j satisfies η=1+nβ, is integral by the subring clause of def-weil-pbc-integral-closure, and lies in E=Q(η). Step 5: multiplicativity and N(a)=a^d from lem-sfb-finite-field-norm-minpoly give n^{p-1}|p, so n=p≥3 and p²|p, a contradiction; p=2 is excluded by n≥3. New node lem-sfb-prime-cyclotomic-degree-norm is unsplit and true, since the minimal polynomial of η-1 is Φ_p(X+1); checked at p=2 (norm -2) and p=3 (X²+3X+3, norm 3).
